landmarks.philo_role: Central result: the unit interval over Cauchy-process reals is uncountable. Resolves Cantor's theorem within ToS without Axiom of Infinity.

checkpoints.our_value: For any enumeration E:nat->CauchyProcess, exists D in [0,1] not equivalent to any E(n). Via shrinking trisection intervals.
checkpoints.reference_value: |[0,1]| = 2^aleph_0 > aleph_0, by diagonal/nested intervals on R

discrepancies: We do not formulate cardinalities; result is constructive avoidance, not cardinal comparison

classical_counterpart.our_statement: forall E : nat -> CauchyProcess, exists D, forall n, ~ process_equiv D (E n)

classical.standard_proof: Cantor's diagonal or nested intervals on complete R
classical.reference: Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, Thm 2.43

comparison.ontological_diff: We use processes (nat->Q) instead of completed reals. No actual infinity assumed.
comparison.proof_method_diff: Trisection intervals guarantee 2/3 of interval is free at each step; classical uses binary nested intervals or diagonal on digits
comparison.strength_detail: We avoid Axiom of Infinity but work over Q-Cauchy processes, not completed reals. Our result is constructive (computes the avoided point) but in a weaker number system.

semantic_intent.purpose: Central uncountability result — proves the process-real continuum is genuinely larger than the naturals
semantic_intent.why_this_formulation: Interval-based trisection avoids digit stability (Qfloor discontinuity); sync invariant 2*delta < w/3 ensures convergence

landmarks.philo_role: Extreme Value Theorem via L5-Resolution: constructive argmax on grid refinement. Demonstrates P4 finite actuality — maximum found by finite algorithm.

checkpoints.our_value: Constructive argmax via L5-Resolution (leftmost index on grid), process converges as Cauchy

classical_counterpart.our_statement: For Lipschitz f on [a,b], sup_process (grid refinement argmax) is Cauchy and stays in [a,b]

classical.statement: f continuous on compact [a,b] => exists x in [a,b]: f(x) = sup f([a,b])
classical.standard_proof: Compactness of [a,b] + continuity => f([a,b]) compact => sup attained

comparison.what_we_share: Maximum is attained on bounded closed interval
comparison.ontological_diff: We compute argmax as limit of grid refinements (process), not by invoking compactness
comparison.proof_method_diff: L5-Resolution selects leftmost maximum on each grid; Lipschitz bound controls grid error
comparison.strength_detail: Constructive algorithm: given f and [a,b], we COMPUTE the argmax process. Classical only asserts existence.

semantic_intent.purpose: Constructive extreme value theorem — finds maximum by grid refinement, not by compactness argument
semantic_intent.why_this_formulation: Index-based argmax avoids Qeq vs Leibniz equality issues; L5 provides deterministic tie-breaking

landmarks.philo_role: Intermediate Value Theorem: epsilon-IVT over Q. Cannot find exact zero (impossible over Q), but finds root process converging to zero.

checkpoints.what: Continuous f with f(a)<0<f(b) has root in (a,b)
checkpoints.our_value: For all eps>0, exists x in [a,b]: |f(x)| < eps. Root converges as Cauchy process.

discrepancies: We find epsilon-approximate roots, not exact zero (impossible over Q)

classical_counterpart.our_statement: forall eps > 0, exists x in [a,b]: |f(x)| < eps (Cauchy process of approximate roots)

classical.statement: f continuous, f(a) < 0 < f(b) => exists c in (a,b): f(c) = 0
classical.standard_proof: Bisection + completeness of R => limit point is exact zero

comparison.ontological_diff: Over Q, f may never be exactly 0. Our root is a process (nat->Q) approaching zero.
comparison.proof_method_diff: Same bisection; we stop at epsilon-approximation, they take the limit
comparison.strength_detail: We guarantee |f(x)| < eps for any eps, not f(x) = 0. This is inherent to working over Q.

semantic_intent.purpose: Epsilon-IVT: constructive root-finding over Q via bisection process
semantic_intent.why_this_formulation: Exact zero impossible over Q; epsilon-IVT is the strongest achievable statement without R completeness

landmarks.philo_role: Constructive proof that positive rationals are countable: explicit bijection N->Q+.

external_validation.classical_ref: Cantor 1874; Enderton, Elements of Set Theory, Ch 6

checkpoints.our_value: Explicit computable bijection N -> Q+, no Axiom of Choice
checkpoints.reference_value: Existence of bijection via diagonal argument, typically uses AC for well-ordering

classical_counterpart.our_statement: Explicit injective enumeration of positive rationals with computable inverse

classical.standard_proof: Cantor's diagonal pairing or Stern-Brocot tree
classical.reference: Enderton, Elements of Set Theory, Ch 6

comparison.ontological_diff: We construct the bijection explicitly; classical asserts existence
comparison.proof_method_diff: Explicit pairing function on coprime pairs
comparison.strength_detail: Fully constructive: no AC, computable bijection

semantic_intent.purpose: Establishes Q is countable — needed for uncountability contrast and PCH
semantic_intent.why_this_formulation: Direct bijection avoids AC; positive rationals suffice for contrast with uncountable [0,1]

landmarks.philo_role: Cantor-Schroeder-Bernstein theorem: injections both ways implies bijection. Key structural result for cardinality theory.
publications: Schroeder 1898, Bernstein 1898; Halmos, Naive Set Theory

external_validation.classical_ref: Schroeder 1898, Bernstein 1898; Halmos, Naive Set Theory, Sec 22

checkpoints.what: Injections A->B and B->A imply bijection A<->B
checkpoints.our_value: Same statement, proved using classic (L3) for orbit classification
checkpoints.reference_value: Same, using LEM for orbit classification

classical_counterpart.our_statement: Injections f:A->B and g:B->A imply exists bijection h:A->B

classical.standard_proof: Partition A into orbits under g(f(-)); each orbit contributes to bijection

comparison.ontological_diff: Minimal — uses classic (L3) which is our LEM
comparison.strength_detail: Formulations are equivalent; both use LEM

semantic_intent.purpose: Foundational set-theoretic tool for cardinality comparisons
semantic_intent.why_this_formulation: Standard CSB; uses classic for orbit classification (unavoidable)

landmarks.philo_role: Heine-Borel compactness: open cover of [a,b] has finite subcover. Proved with Lebesgue number assumption.

checkpoints.our_value: Open cover with Lebesgue number assumption has finite subcover
checkpoints.reference_value: Every open cover of [a,b] in R has finite subcover (no extra assumptions)

discrepancies: Our version requires Lebesgue number as hypothesis (cannot derive it over Q)

classical_counterpart.our_statement: Open cover with Lebesgue number lambda > 0 has finite subcover of size ceil((b-a)/lambda)

classical.statement: Every open cover of [a,b] in R has finite subcover
classical.standard_proof: Bisection + completeness => Lebesgue number exists => finite subcover

comparison.what_we_share: Finite subcover extraction from open cover
comparison.ontological_diff: Classical derives Lebesgue number from completeness; we assume it
comparison.proof_method_diff: Given Lebesgue number, finite cover is straightforward grid argument
comparison.strength_detail: We need Lebesgue number as hypothesis; classical derives it from completeness. [0,1] over Q is not compact.
gaps_vs_classical: Cannot derive Lebesgue number without R completeness
advantages_vs_classical: Explicit finite cover size bound: ceil((b-a)/lambda)

semantic_intent.purpose: Compactness with Lebesgue number — strongest Heine-Borel achievable over Q
semantic_intent.why_this_formulation: [0,1] over Q is genuinely not compact; Lebesgue number assumption is the honest bridge

landmarks.philo_role: Principle 1 (Everything is a system): no level contains itself. Structural resolution of Russell's paradox — self-membership is impossible by construction.

external_validation.classical_ref: Zermelo 1930; Kunen, Set Theory, Ch I.6

checkpoints.our_value: Derived from Level hierarchy: level_lt is irreflexive by induction
checkpoints.reference_value: Axiom of Regularity: every non-empty set has element disjoint from itself

classical_counterpart.our_statement: forall L, ~ (L << L) — no level is strictly below itself

classical.statement: Axiom of Regularity: forall S, S != {} => exists x in S, x cap S = {}

comparison.ontological_diff: We DERIVE it from Level induction; ZFC POSTULATES it as axiom
comparison.proof_method_diff: Induction on Level type (well-founded by construction)
comparison.strength_detail: Derived theorem vs postulated axiom. Our hierarchy makes self-membership structurally impossible.

semantic_intent.purpose: Foundation of ToS hierarchy — levels cannot self-contain, blocking Russell's paradox
semantic_intent.why_this_formulation: Level is inductive (L1, LS L) so irreflexivity follows by structural induction

landmarks.philo_role: Demonstration that Russell's paradox is structurally impossible: cannot construct a criterion whose domain equals its codomain level.

external_validation.classical_ref: Russell 1901; ZFC resolves via Comprehension restriction

checkpoints.what: Russell's set {x : x not in x} cannot be formed
checkpoints.our_value: Structurally impossible: criterion domain and codomain must be at different levels
checkpoints.reference_value: ZFC restricts Comprehension to subsets of existing sets

classical_counterpart.our_statement: Cannot construct criterion C at level L that examines level L elements (type error)

classical.statement: Axiom of Comprehension restricted: {x in A : phi(x)} for existing A

comparison.ontological_diff: ZFC restricts formation rules; ToS makes self-reference impossible by level structure
comparison.proof_method_diff: Level hierarchy prevents domain=codomain; ZFC prevents unrestricted comprehension
comparison.strength_detail: Structural impossibility vs syntactic restriction. Our levels make the paradox untypeable.

semantic_intent.purpose: Demonstrates that ToS hierarchy structurally prevents Russell-type paradoxes
semantic_intent.why_this_formulation: Direct proof that self-referential criterion construction fails at type level

landmarks.philo_role: Banach fixed-point theorem: iteration of contraction mapping produces Cauchy sequence converging to unique fixed point.

checkpoints.what: Contraction on complete metric space has unique fixed point
checkpoints.our_value: Iteration of contraction (rate < 1) on Q produces Cauchy sequence; convergence rate is geometric
checkpoints.reference_value: Same with convergence to actual fixed point in complete space

classical_counterpart.our_statement: is_contraction f r, 0 < r < 1 => iterate f x0 is Cauchy (convergence rate r^n)

classical.statement: T contraction on complete (X,d) => exists unique x*: T(x*) = x*, and T^n(x0) -> x*
classical.standard_proof: Geometric series bound on d(x_n, x_{n+1})

comparison.ontological_diff: We prove Cauchy property; classical proves convergence to fixed point in complete space
comparison.proof_method_diff: Same geometric bound; we stop at Cauchy, they invoke completeness for limit
comparison.strength_detail: Equivalent modulo completeness — our Cauchy IS their convergence in our framework
gaps_vs_classical: No explicit fixed point (only Cauchy sequence)
advantages_vs_classical: Used by ReasoningConvergence.v for AI pipeline

semantic_intent.purpose: Banach fixed-point — foundation for convergence analysis, used by ReasoningConvergence and GradientDescent
semantic_intent.why_this_formulation: Contraction rate as Q parameter; Cauchy is the natural completeness-free convergence notion

landmarks.philo_role: Bolzano-Weierstrass: bounded sequence has convergent (Cauchy) subsequence.

checkpoints.what: Every bounded sequence in R has convergent subsequence
checkpoints.our_value: Bounded Q-process has Cauchy subsequential process (bisection extraction)
checkpoints.reference_value: Every bounded real sequence has convergent subsequence

classical_counterpart.our_statement: Bounded process has Cauchy cluster point process

classical.statement: Every bounded sequence in R has convergent subsequence

comparison.ontological_diff: Cauchy cluster point vs actual limit
comparison.proof_method_diff: Same bisection; we prove Cauchy, they prove convergence

semantic_intent.purpose: Sequential compactness for bounded processes — key analysis tool
semantic_intent.why_this_formulation: Bisection interval halving extracts cluster point as Cauchy process

landmarks.philo_role: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus on grid: integral of derivative recovers function increment up to grid error.

checkpoints.what: Integral of f' on [a,b] equals f(b) - f(a)
checkpoints.our_value: Grid Riemann sum of f' approximates f(b)-f(a) with error controlled by grid size and Lipschitz constant

discrepancies: Our version is approximate (grid-based); classical is exact limit

classical_counterpart.our_statement: Riemann sum of f' on N-grid approximates f(b)-f(a) with error O(1/N)

classical.statement: If F' = f continuous on [a,b], then int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a)
classical.standard_proof: Mean Value Theorem + limit of Riemann sums

comparison.ontological_diff: We use finite grid sums; classical uses limit of Riemann sums
comparison.strength_detail: As grid refines (N->inf), our error -> 0, recovering classical FTC

semantic_intent.purpose: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus — connects Riemann sums to antiderivatives with explicit error
semantic_intent.why_this_formulation: Grid-based avoids limits; error bound is explicit and computable

landmarks.philo_role: Process Continuum Hypothesis: every closed binary collection is either enumerable or contains a perfect subset. The classical CH 'dissolves' — the question transforms into a structural classification.

checkpoints.what: Is there a set S with aleph_0 < |S| < 2^aleph_0?
checkpoints.our_value: Question dissolves: every closed collection is enumerable OR has perfect subset (no intermediate)

discrepancies: Classical CH is about cardinality; PCH reframes as structural classification

classical_counterpart.our_statement: Every closed binary collection is either enumerable or contains a perfect subset

classical.statement: There is no set S with aleph_0 < |S| < 2^aleph_0 (CH); independent of ZFC
classical.standard_proof: Godel: L model satisfies CH. Cohen: forcing produces ~CH model.

comparison.ontological_diff: Classical CH is about cardinal numbers; PCH is about structural classification of process collections
comparison.proof_method_diff: We prove a dichotomy theorem; they show independence
comparison.strength_detail: PCH is a different question than CH. It dissolves rather than resolves the continuum problem.

semantic_intent.purpose: Dissolution of the continuum hypothesis — reframes cardinality question as structural dichotomy
semantic_intent.why_this_formulation: Binary processes give natural countable/uncountable classification without cardinal arithmetic

landmarks.philo_role: Novel result: eigenspace spectrum is either discrete (enumerable) or continuous (perfect subset). Connects PCH to quantum mechanics — observable = process, measurement = approximation.

checkpoints.our_value: Every spectrum is either discrete (enumerable eigenvalues) or continuous (has perfect subset)
checkpoints.reference_value: In functional analysis: spectrum = point + continuous + residual (Dunford-Schwartz)

discrepancies: Classical spectral theory has 3-part decomposition; ours is 2-part (from PCH)

classical_counterpart.our_statement: Eigenspace collection is either enumerable or contains perfect subset (dichotomy from PCH)

classical.statement: Spectrum of operator = point spectrum + continuous spectrum + residual spectrum
classical.reference: Reed-Simon, Methods of Mathematical Physics, Vol I

comparison.ontological_diff: We classify by cardinality structure (PCH dichotomy); classical classifies by operator properties
comparison.proof_method_diff: PCH dichotomy applied to eigenspace collection
comparison.strength_detail: Different framework — our dichotomy is structural, theirs is analytic
advantages_vs_classical: Derives from PCH (no operator theory needed)

semantic_intent.purpose: Bridge from PCH to physics: spectrum classification follows from process continuum hypothesis
semantic_intent.why_this_formulation: Direct consequence of PCH applied to eigenspace collection

landmarks.philo_role: Type Safety (Progress + Preservation) for ToS-Lang: well-typed expressions don't get stuck. Foundation for verified compilation.

external_validation.classical_ref: Wright-Felleisen 1994; Pierce, Types and Programming Languages, Ch 8

checkpoints.our_value: type_safety: well-typed expression either is value, steps, or is benign-stuck (EResolve on non-const)
checkpoints.reference_value: Well-typed term is value or steps (2-way progress)

discrepancies: Our progress is 3-way (value/step/benign_stuck) due to L5-Resolution semantics

classical_counterpart.our_statement: Well-typed expression: value OR steps OR benign_stuck (EResolve on non-const); type preserved under steps

classical.statement: Progress: well-typed closed term is value or steps. Preservation: step preserves type.

comparison.what_we_share: Induction on typing derivation for both progress and preservation
comparison.ontological_diff: ToS-Lang includes L5-Resolution operator (EResolve) which creates benign_stuck states
comparison.proof_method_diff: Same structural induction; extra case for EResolve/EObserve
comparison.strength_detail: Standard type safety with ToS-specific extension for L5-Resolution

semantic_intent.purpose: Type Safety for ToS-Lang: ensures well-typed programs are safe (don't get stuck)
semantic_intent.why_this_formulation: 3-way progress (value/step/benign_stuck) handles L5-Resolution gracefully

landmarks.philo_role: L5 Resolution (Law of Order): non-empty list with total order always has unique minimum. Core mechanism for deterministic selection in ToS.

checkpoints.our_value: l5_resolve_gen on non-empty list with DecTotalOrder returns Some (minimum element)
checkpoints.reference_value: Well-ordering: every set can be well-ordered (but uses AC)

discrepancies: L5 is constructive and deterministic; well-ordering uses AC

classical_counterpart.our_statement: l5_resolve_gen returns Some for non-empty list over DecTotalOrder

classical.statement: Every set can be well-ordered (Zermelo); every finite set has minimum under total order
classical.standard_proof: Zermelo well-ordering uses AC; finite case by induction

comparison.what_we_share: Selection of minimum from ordered collection
comparison.ontological_diff: L5 is a PRINCIPLE (not derived from AC); operates on finite lists only
comparison.proof_method_diff: Structural induction on list; comparison-based selection
comparison.strength_detail: L5 is a foundational principle of ToS, not a theorem. It grounds determinism.

semantic_intent.purpose: L5 Resolution: deterministic minimum selection — foundation for all 'choice' in ToS
semantic_intent.why_this_formulation: DecTotalOrder + list = minimal interface for deterministic selection without AC

landmarks.philo_role: Second law of thermodynamics derived from L1 (symmetry) without Past Hypothesis. L1 → doubly stochastic T → majorization → Schur → S non-decreasing. Resolves Wolpert-Rovelli circle.
Every distinction is a conserved quantity. Energy, charge, momentum, information conservation as L5 instances. Memory = special case.
P4 (inexhaustibility) derived as theorem from combinatorial growth. Analysis (K linear) + synthesis (K²/2 quadratic) → potential always exceeds actualization. Void inexhaustible = constructive proof.
S = k·ln(2)·|D(K)| exact from L2+L3 (binarity). Each distinction = 1 bit. Shannon derived, not postulated.
Minkowski metric ds² = dt² - dx² derived from observer structure. No absolute simultaneity: two observers share distinction at different stages. Causal cone from graph distance.
Hydrogen atom on lattice: H(M,K,i,j) ∈ Q. Kinetic (tridiag) + Coulomb (-2M/(i+1)). E₂/E₁ → 1/4 as M → ∞. Polynomial correction = critical (dense spectrum).
Coulomb integral J = 5α/8 exact over Q. He CI with 2-STO basis, all matrix elements rational. E_He = -729/256 Ha (1.93% from NIST).
First heteronuclear molecule verified over Q. HF: α_H=1, α_F=27/10. Potential energy curve with minimum at R=1.7. Polar bond verified (Δχ > 0.5).
Sharkovskii theorem: period-3 implies all periods. Complete for PL maps (all orbits ∈ Q) and general continuous case (covering lemma). Extensions: fails on circle and in dim ≥ 2.
Process classification strictly finer than topological entropy. Witness: diag(2,1) vs diag(2,-1) — same λ_max=2 but different tr(M^K). The journey contains more than the destination.
Graphene: 2-sublattice honeycomb → off-diagonal T → tr=0 (bipartite) → gap=0 at Dirac point. D(E) ∝ |E|. Berry phase = π. BN gap from broken sublattice symmetry.
BCS gap Δ from Padé exp over Q. Cooper pair = bound state from any V<0. T_BCS = [[ε,Δ],[Δ,-ε]], tr=0. Condensation energy = -NΔ²/2.
Observer = witness function mapping distinctions to observations. Witnesses are unique, grow with D(K), are preserved by L5. Time = nat index on observation process.
Level ≅ nat (bijection proved). Peano axioms = L5 hierarchy properties. Natural numbers derived from distinction structure, not postulated.
